transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-10 15:30 PDT | Duration: 42 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Sable Orbit), Evan (CTO), Lina (DevOps), Samir (Product)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro from our side — I'm Maya Chen, I'm the AE covering infra customers, and Diego is our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Priya: Hey Maya, hi Diego, yeah thanks. quick context — we're building a customer-facing assistant that needs sub-200ms p95 on short queries and secure handling of PII.
[00:23] Diego: Great — a couple quick clarifying q's if that's ok? are you currently running anything in prod today for LLMs or is this a greenfield?
[00:30] Evan: We have a small pilot with another vendor but it's mostly eval. it's not meeting our latency targets and cost is creeping. we want options: hosted to move fast, dedicated for predictability, or private for compliance.
[00:45] Maya: Totally. the typical path we see is start PLG/self-serve hosted to get time-to-first-token fast — free credits, SDKs, a simple API key — then consider dedicated if you need reserved GPUs or private if you need VPC/KMS and strict audit controls.
[01:05] Priya: Walk us through the actual time-to-first-token. like, from sign up to the first successful inference call.
[01:12] Maya: On average for teams we track: sign-up + SDK install + one sample call can be as little as 20-45 minutes. with our free credits you can actually get a full test suite in a day. Diego, want to add numbers?
[01:25] Diego: Yeah — in our quickstart flow, with the Node/Python SDK and sample prompts, median time-to-first-token is ~12 minutes for someone who has dev access. if you include CI pipelines and artifacting, say a dev can iterate an hour. for latency, it depends on model variant — for an open Llama-like model quantized vs a larger dense model, p95 will vary a lot.
[01:45] Lina: When you say hosted, where is data going? we have to ensure no PII is retained and customer data residency is honored.
[01:52] Maya: Good point. hosted runs in our managed cloud regions; by default we don't persist prompts beyond short-term logs used for debugging. we have configurable retention and a compliance package — Diego will share the SOC2 report, and we support KMS integrations for encrypting data at rest for Private deployments.
[02:10] Samir: Who in our org signs the DPA? and does Redwood support SAML SSO for team access?
[02:17] Maya: Yes, enterprise DPA and SSO (SAML/SCIM) are supported. for PLG accounts, standard terms apply, but we can escalate to enterprise licensing for private deployments.
[02:26] Evan: For the dedicated option — how deterministic is throughput? if we lock a reserved pool what's the upper bound tokens per second?
[02:34] Diego: Reserved capacity gives predictable throughput; it's basically a fleet of GPUs with autoscaling and burst allowances. throughput depends on model & sequence length; we can size based on your concurrency targets. We'll propose two profiles after we run a 10k-token synthetic bench.
[02:48] Priya: Sounds good. on the privacy front we need KMS integration and long-term audit logs. we also need the KV cache behavior documented — our legal team wants to know what gets cached and for how long.
[02:59] Maya: We have docs on KV cache; by default KV cache is ephemeral per-request and not retained beyond session unless you enable persistent caching. we'll send explicit docs and an infra diagram.
[03:12] Diego: Quick technical note: if you need lowest latency we recommend smaller context models with optimized kernels and continuous batching tuned to your request pattern. For highest throughput per dollar, quantized model variants on Dedicated are typically best.
[03:28] Priya: Any concerns about hallucination or output quality regressions when you switch quantized variants?
[03:34] Diego: Yep — there is a tradeoff. Redwood Optimize gives suggestions and we can run evals against your prompt sets to measure regressions. we can do a canary where we route 5-10% of traffic to a cheaper quantized profile and compare.
[03:50] Samir: Ok, for pilot we'd like to test: (1) hosted quickstart to verify baseline integration and time-to-first-token, (2) small dedicated pool for throughput testing, (3) a private pilot in QA for compliance checks. is that a reasonable sequence?
[04:04] Maya: That's exactly the pattern we recommend. start with hosted for fast feedback, then move to dedicated for predictability, and only go private if controls demand it.
[04:12] Priya: Pricing? how are credits applied and what's the path to reserved capacity pricing?
[04:18] Maya: Credits are applied to your hosted usage; for Dedicated we do committed monthly/annual contracts. we'll share a simple pricing sheet. typical pilots are small monthly commits.
[04:29] Evan: One more — network egress. if we run private on-prem, is traffic fully internal or do we still phone home to Redwood control plane?
[04:37] Diego: For Private/VPC deployments, the control plane can be customer-managed and audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. there is an optional air-gapped package where the inference plane is fully on-prem and the control plane can be isolated.
[04:51] Priya: That helps. in terms of onboarding we want an estimate for the time it takes to run the three-phase pilot you described.
[04:57] Maya: Hosted quickstart: 1-3 days to first meaningful results. Dedicated scoping & sizing: 1-2 weeks to provision and run meaningful benches. Private pilot (depends heavily on infra & legal): 3-8 weeks typical.
[05:15] Lina: For the hosted benchmark can you run with our synthetic dataset? we can provide a zipped payload.
[05:20] Diego: Absolutely — drop it in a signed S3 presigned link and we'll run both latency and cost estimates. we prefer redacted PII but realistic distribution.
[05:30] Priya: ok sending that. also send over SDK examples for streaming responses and function/tool calling — we rely on structured output.
[05:36] Maya: Will do. we'll include the Node and Python streaming examples and a short how-to for function calling.
[05:44] Evan: Are there guardrails for rate limiting and throttling? we need graceful degradation strategies.
[05:50] Diego: Yes — per-route quotas, token-based rate limits, and fallback policies. you can configure automatic fallback to a smaller model or a cached summary.
[06:00] Priya: We've had issues with ambiguous attribution in vendor transcripts — how good is Redwood's output for tool-calling determinism?
[06:06] Diego: It depends on model and prompt engineering; our SDK supports a structured response mode to reduce ambiguity and we have built-in evals to catch regressions.
[06:15] Samir: Let's recap and next steps?
[06:18] Maya: Recap: Maya will send SOC2, infra diagram, pricing sheet and SDK examples. Diego will run hosted vs dedicated synthetic bench once Priya shares payload. Sable Orbit to confirm pilot timeline and prompt sets. We'll schedule a scoping call in two weeks.
[06:36] Priya: Works for us. thanks all.
[06:39] Evan: Thanks.
[06:41] Maya: Great, we'll follow up via email with the docs and a calendar invite for the scoping call.

Notes/Artifacts referenced: SOC2 whitepaper (link to be shared), quickstart SDK repo (node/python), sample benchmark template (spreadsheet), pilot scoping doc.

End of transcript.
